en: The Sūtra of the Girl Sumati, translated by the Wu-period Yuezhi Upāsaka Zhi Qian.
Thus have I heard: At one time, the Buddha was staying in the city of Śrāvastī within the kingdom of Kośala. There was an elder...

He was named Anāthapiṇḍika, and he had a daughter named Sumati. This girl had long cultivated sublime causes; she was exceptionally extraordinary, having received the Buddha’s noble conduct and dwelling in the profound chamber of a tranquil mind.

At that time, in the city of Pūrṇavardhana, there was an elder named Pūrṇabhadra who had traveled far across various kingdoms in search of a bride of excellent qualities. Consequently, he entered the city of Śrāvastī and met with Viśākhā; they opened their hearts to one another, and after a long period of separation, they conversed with the utmost sincerity and joy.

At that time, the maiden Sumati, because her father was of the same lineage as the Honored One, briefly went forth to pay her respects; her countenance was radiant and her myriad features were all beautiful, her face like the white moon at its fullness, her eyes like the many stars shining brightly in the night.
Pūrṇa said to Bhāradvāja,
"Whose daughter is this woman?
Bhāradvāja replied:
"This girl is indeed my daughter.
Upon hearing this, Pūrṇa rejoiced and exclaimed to himself, "I have been acquainted with you for many years;

our bond of friendship does not permit outsiders. I have a young son whom I am just now seeking a wife for, though no specific match has yet been decided upon. This young daughter of yours would make an excellent partner for him."
Pūrṇa said, "This matter should not be handled in such a way.
Pūrṇadhana lamented to himself:
"Why is it that the matter is not appropriate in this way?
Is it because our ancestral lineages are of unequal standing, or because our current livelihoods are unequal?
You are also noble, honored, wealthy, and powerful; I too am noble, honored, wealthy, and powerful. Why is it that the matter is not appropriate in this way?"
Bhṛṅgī replied again:

"My daughter has long been mindful of the Buddha and has maintained the fasts and precepts; your family, however, has inherited the worship of external deities and partakes in blood sacrifices. Because our lineages and affiliations differ in this way, such a marriage is not appropriate."
Pūrṇa said to Bhāradvāja:

"The objects of worship in your family you shall honor separately, and the objects of worship in my family we shall honor separately; though our objects of worship differ, what prevents each person from honoring their own preference?"
At that time, Pindola was unwilling to grant his consent, yet he could not easily refuse the request:
"I demand ten thousand catties of your gold, a hundred measures of bright pearls, dragon livers as a gift, and phoenix gall for the banquet; if you can provide these, only then may we part."
Upon hearing this, Pūrṇadhana was both startled and delighted, and he vowed:
"I am able to provide for it.
Vāsiṣṭha spoke again:
"I was merely joking; this was not my sincere intention. We must first consult the Buddha before we can proceed.
Thereupon, Pindola went to question the Buddha, saying:
"World-Honored One!..."
Now, the maiden Sumati has been sought in marriage by the elder Pūrṇa of the city of Pūrṇabhadra;
should she be given to him, or should she not?
The Buddha said,
"If the maiden Sumati marries into that country, she will deliver a vast number of people beyond measure.
Thereupon, Pindola returned and spoke to Pūrṇa:
"Prepare the rites and ceremonies of your house in fifteen days' time.
Upon hearing this, Pūrṇadhana was filled with joy and crawled back home on his hands and knees.

At that time, the city of Pūrṇavardhana and Śrāvastī were separated by three thousand two hundred li; within that distance, Pūrṇadhana led ten thousand chariots, with dragon-horses flanking his retinue. Banners and streamers reached the clouds, the sound of bells shook the earth, court ladies supported the wheels, and servants attended at intervals.

At that time, Anāthapiṇḍika first had twelve kinds of jeweled chariots crafted for his daughter. He first lined the interior with red lotuses and covered the exterior with *maṇi* gems; they were overlaid with gold and draped with white silver, featuring variegated patterns of amber, interspersed with coral, lapis lazuli, *śaṅkha*, and agate, and inlaid with *sphatika*. They were adorned with the shimmering luster of lapis lazuli, further embellished with layers of purple-gold *parihāra* suspended and cascading upward. Thus, their brilliance mutually stimulated one another and their radiance illuminated each other; those who viewed them from afar could not perceive whether shadows shifted from east to west, while those who looked closely could not help but feel their eyes spinning in dizziness.
At that time, there was a long-standing regulation in the city of Pūrṇabhadra:

"If a woman from within this city marries into another country, she shall be subject to severe punishment; likewise, if a wife is sought from another country and brought back here, she shall also be subject to severe punishment."

If anyone violates this decree, they shall be compelled to provide sustenance for six thousand Brahmins and satisfy their desires; as for the food of these Brahmins, pork shall serve as their soup and threefold-distilled liquor as their wine.
Pūrṇa, realizing he had violated the precepts, invited a great assembly of masters to a spacious courtyard and ordered the maiden Sumati to pay homage to them. Sumati said:

"Though I am a woman, my will is firm and cannot be bent. These followers of the Brahmans are no different from young oxen; with their five hideous forms, they greedily crave delicious flavors, possessing neither shame nor modesty—how are they any different from beasts?"
"I would rather have my body mutilated into five stumps than pay homage to this man.
At that time, the six thousand brahmins heard this and were simultaneously incensed, saying:
"Where did he find a commoner’s small slave girl to come here and insult us?"
Thereupon, they gathered from various places where they were seated, setting a date and choosing an hour with the intent to come and slaughter Pūrṇa along with his five clans.
Pūrṇa then shut himself up in a high tower, crying out to Heaven and lamenting his injustice:
"Why do you seek this [destruction] to ruin my five clans?"
He was thus consumed by grief and could find no way to relieve himself.
At that time, Subhadra flew up onto the upper story of the building and, seeing Pūrṇabhadra looking haggard with sorrow, spoke to him:
"Have you been plundered by bandits, or have you died and not been buried? Why do you wear such a look of grief?"
Pūrṇadhana replied, "It is not a matter of death or thieves;
rather, since yesterday I took a wife for my son, I have brought disgrace upon my teachers and my five lineages, and because of this I am so distressed that I have no way to relieve myself."
At that time, Subhadra said to Pūrṇabhadra,
"From where did you take your wife?
Pūrṇabhadra replied:
"Anāthapiṇḍika’s daughter from the city of Śrāvastī.
When Subhadra heard this, he was greatly startled and terrified, saying:
"Your wife is now coming here; we shall surely meet with great misfortune."
Pūrṇa asked, "How do you know this?
Subhadra replied:

"Formerly, together with Śāriputra, I went with his youngest novice disciple named Kuṇḍala, who was only three or four years old, to beg for alms north of the Snowy Mountains. Each of us obtained one bowl, whereupon I flew high up and arrived at the shore of Lake Anavatapta."
At that time, there were devas, nāgas, and spirits by the side of the pond who shielded and protected the water, not allowing me to approach it.
At that moment, the śrāmaṇera Kundo also flew over, whereupon he was even more joyful and exclaimed:
"Excellent! Wonderful!"
"Sitting upon a golden stand, he offered his practice with such total devotion that in a mere instant, he transcended the four formless realms and returned to his original place.
If even this youngest śrāmaṇera possesses such divine virtue, how much more so must it be for the Great Master whom he serves?"
Pūrṇa asked, "Can that teacher be seen?
Subhadra replied:
“If you wish to see that Great Teacher, you must seek out the maiden Sumati.
Thereupon, Pūrṇa descended from the upper story and, with respectful intent, said to the maiden Sumati:
“Is it possible for me to see the teacher whom you now serve?”

Sumati said, "If the elder changes his mind and turns his thoughts toward deeply taking refuge in virtue, I shall apply fragrant powder to my body for the elder and ascend the tower to go and invite him from afar."
At that time, the maiden Sumati anointed her body with fragrant oil, ascended to the top of a high tower, and addressed the Buddha from afar, saying:
"World-Honored One!

This maiden is now in peril, being oppressed by various malevolent spirits. I pray that the World-Honored One, in your great kindness and great compassion, will rescue me from this danger and distress."
Thereupon, fragrances like clouds proceeded to the Jetavana Monastery.
Seeing such extraordinary fragrances as he had never seen before, Ānanda addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!”
“From where does this extraordinary fragrance come?

The Buddha said, “This fragrance is the scent sent by the Buddha. Now, the daughter Sumati is in the city of Pūrṇabhadra and is being oppressed by various heterodox paths; she has now dispatched this fragrance to invite me and you all.”
He quickly struck the gong to assemble the multitude in the Universal Assembly Hall and addressed them, saying:

"The maiden Sumati is currently in the city of Pūrṇabhadda, being oppressed by various heterodox paths. I have now dispatched this messenger to invite the Buddha and his assembly. If there are those among you who have attained supernatural powers and transformations, please take a tally; those who have not shall remain silent."

At that time, among the assembly were Cūḍapanthaka, the Buddha’s son Rāhula, Subhūti, Śāriputra, Kāśyapa, Maudgalyāyana, and others. Among those who had not yet received full ordination was a śrāmaṇera named Kṣemaka, who first took up the tally-stick to oversee the selection for the path of the sages.
Ānanda said to the Buddha, "In that land there must be no large vessels for cooking food; therefore, send Qianxu to carry a cauldron ahead on the road.

Although Qianxu was but a messenger, he was equipped with the five supernatural powers; he carried a great cauldron of ten thousand *hu* on his back and held a great ladle of a hundred *hu* in his hand, leaping high into the air and flying directly toward that land.
At that time, Pūrṇadhana, from atop his tower, saw [him] from afar and said to Sumati:
"I see a man coming through the air, carrying a great cauldron of a thousand *khu* on his back and holding a great ladle of a hundred *khu* in his hand; is he not your teacher?"
Sumati said, “This is not my teacher;
this is a servant among the community of monks named Ghaṭīkāra. As the World-Honored One wishes to arrive, he has been sent to carry the cooking pots ahead on the road.”
At that time, the śrāmaṇera Kuṇḍopadhānīya next manifested five hundred flowering trees; he sat cross-legged atop each one and, leaping high into the air, flew toward that land as well.

From atop the Pūrṇabhadda tower, he saw them from afar and said to Sumati, "I see five hundred flowering trees, and upon them there are people sitting cross-legged who are coming through the air; are they not your teachers?"
Sumati said, "This is not my teacher;
this is Śāriputra’s youngest śrāmaṇera, named Kṣemaka.

Then Cūḍapanthaka next manifested five hundred lions; with a single loud roar, they flew down and prostrated themselves, while he sat cross-legged upon them. Leaping high into the air, he flew directly toward that kingdom.
From atop the Pūrṇadhana tower, he saw them from afar and asked Sumati:

"I see five hundred lions that, upon being called out with a single cry, fly down and prostrate themselves; there is a man sitting cross-legged upon them, coming through the air—is this not your teacher?"
"This is not my teacher; this is the Tathāgata’s disciple Cūḍapanthaka.

Then Rāhula, the son of the Buddha, arrived later and transformed himself into five hundred kings of the garuḍas, with a person sitting cross-legged atop each one. He leaped high into the air and flew directly toward that country.
From atop the Pūrṇadhana tower,
he saw them from afar and asked Sumati,
"I see five hundred kings of the garuḍas, with a man seated upon them in the full lotus posture, coming through the air; is he not your teacher?"
The girl Sumati said, "This is not my teacher;
this is Rāhula, a son of the Buddha and a disciple of the Tathāgata.

Subhūti then successively manifested five hundred elephant kings, each with six tusks and adorned with golden saddles. Men sat upon them in the full lotus posture as they leaped up and soared through the void toward that land.
From atop the Pūrṇadhana tower, he saw them from afar and asked Sumati,
"I see five hundred elephant kings, each with six tusks and draped in golden saddles, with men seated upon them in the full lotus posture, coming through the air— is this your teacher?"
"This is not my teacher; this is the Tathāgata’s disciple, Subhūti.
Maudgalyāyana followed next, transformed himself into a mountain of the seven treasures, sat upon it in the full lotus posture, and leaping high into the air, flew directly toward that land.

From atop the Pūrṇadhana tower, he saw them from afar and asked Sumati, "I see a mountain made of the seven treasures, and upon it is a person sitting cross-legged who comes through the air; is this your teacher?"
The girl Sumati said, “This is not my teacher;
this is Maudgalyāyana, a disciple of the Tathāgata endowed with supernormal powers.

Then the Elder Mahākāśyapa arrived later; he manifested himself as five hundred great nāgas, each with seven heads, ascending into the sky by day. Standing atop them, he sat cross-legged and leaped high into the air, flying directly toward that country.

From atop the Pūrṇadhana tower, he saw them from afar and asked the girl Sumati, "I see five hundred great nāgas, each with seven heads, ascending into the heavens by day and coming through the void of space; are these your teachers?"
Sumati said, "This is not my teacher;
this is the Elder Mahākāśyapa, the foremost disciple of the Tathāgata.
Thereupon, the maiden Sumati spoke these verses to the elder:
“My Teacher shall now arrive; his radiance is beyond compare.
Elder, keep this single-mindedly in mind; do not harbor other thoughts.

At that time, the Tathāgata, knowing the minds of sentient beings and that the opportune moment had arrived, donned his saṃghāṭī robe and appeared in mid-air at a height of seven tala trees above the ground, his body the color of purple-gold with a brilliant, soaring luster.

Ajñāta-kauṇḍinya was on the left of the Tathāgata, and Śāriputra was on the right of the Tathāgata; Ānanda, sustained by the Buddha’s majestic spiritual power, was again on the left of the Tathāgata. The remaining bhikṣus manifested hundreds of thousands of kinds of supernatural transformations, filling the void like drifting clouds as they proceeded to that place.
Ājñāta-kauṇḍinya transformed himself into the Moon Deva-son, and Śāriputra transformed himself into the Sun Deva-son;
the remaining bhikṣus, moreover, some transformed themselves into Dhṛtarāṣṭra, some into Virūḍhaka,
and others into Asura kings or Gandharva kings, arraying their drums and military forces at all times.

The *asura* kings vied with one another to rise up; the *asura* king was to serve as the General of the Eastern Wing as the Lord Who Subdues Māra, while the Universal Monarch (*cakravartin*) was to serve as the General of the Western Wing as the Duke Who Stabilizes Māra.
The Gandharva King, grasping ten billion ghost-soldiers in his hand, was to serve as the rear guard for the retreat.
The Heavenly King Śakra was to serve as the Chief Registrar of the Outer Army, and the Heavenly King Brahmā...
He served as the General Superintendent of the Central Army; Mañjuśrī acted as the Minister of Defense for the Tathāgata, commanding both internal and external affairs.
Leading the assembled forces with a single mind, they rose up together.
Guhyapāda the Malla held a vajra-pestle in his hand, acting as the Tathāgata’s protector at his side, while the celestial Māra Pāpīyān held a lapis lazuli lute in his hand.
To praise the Great Dharma, King Vaiśravaṇa held a great parasol made of the seven treasures directly above the Tathāgata,
while all the other worthy sages remained in the void, performing songs and music.

At that time, the Tathāgata likewise manifested signs of supernatural transformation; hundreds of thousands of kinds of sounds resounded, bells chimed, and the earth shook. At that moment, he further manifested signs of supernatural transformation: sometimes entering the Fire-King Samādhi, he raised smoke and sent forth flames; sometimes entering the Water-King Samādhi, he caused sand to fly and waves to surge; or again, he transformed himself into a thunder god with flashing lightning, or produced flying frost and rising hailstones.

At that time, clouds swirled from the ten directions, heaven and earth tilted and turned, a hundred rivers flowed westward, and the suspended light sank in the east; with such spiritual power as this, where could he not be served?

At that time, the six thousand non-Buddhists were deeply moved by his spiritual transformations; he caused the maiden Sumati to attain the clear and penetrating Dharma-eye, and eighty-four thousand people in the city simultaneously attained the Way.
At that time, the Tathāgata withdrew his assembly of noble disciples and returned to the Jeta Grove Monastery. Ānanda knelt with palms joined and addressed the Buddha, saying:
"World-Honored One!"

By what causes and conditions was this girl Sumati born constantly into a great wealthy family; and why, while amidst the path of the net of heterodoxy, did she not merely change her female body but now attain the Dharma-eye, such that all the people within the city have likewise attained the Way?
"I only pray that the World-Honored One will explain the causes from his past lives.
The Buddha said to Ānanda:
"Listen attentively, listen attentively; I shall explain it for you."
In the past, during the time of Kāśyapa Buddha, there was a princess who, from atop a high tower, made this vast and solemn vow:

"May I always be born into a great and wealthy family; may I always encounter the Buddhas; may my mind of giving to sentient beings never regress; and may I not remain in a female body, but immediately attain the Dharma-eye. Thereupon, all the people within the city also made such vast and solemn vows.
"Because Chong accumulated great merit through the performance of the Great Fast and built up virtue over time, by these causes and conditions he has now encountered me and shall deliver all beings.
At that time, Ānanda!
One must not fail to make the great vows for the future, and those who hear this must not fail to assist."
“The princess of that time was none other than the present-day daughter Sumati;
the citizens of the city were the present eighty-four thousand people.
The bhikṣus, bhikṣuṇīs, upāsakas, upāsikās, and the eight classes of beings, including devas and nāga kings, having heard this sutra, rejoiced and paid homage, vowing to practice it accordingly.
The Sūtra of the Girl Sumati
